overview.text: The Protestant Reformation was a sixteenth-century movement that challenged the authority and practices of the Roman Catholic Church and produced new Christian churches. In 1517, Martin Luther circulated his Ninety-Five Theses against the sale of indulgences in German lands. He argued that salvation depended on faith and gave the Bible priority over church tradition. His ideas spread through print and debate, though reformers did not agree on every doctrine. John Calvin became another influential reformer, while Henry VIII broke England’s political ties with Rome. Catholic leaders also pursued reforms of their own in response. The result was a lasting division within western Christianity.

key_facts.text: Martin Luther circulated the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 to challenge indulgences.
Luther emphasized faith and the authority of scripture.
John Calvin published his Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536.
Henry VIII broke England’s ties with the pope in the 1530s.
The familiar story that Luther nailed the theses to a church door is historically disputed.

overview.text: Jovenel Moïse was president of Haiti from February 2017 until his assassination in July 2021. Before entering national politics, he worked in agriculture and became associated with banana production. He ran with the Haitian Tèt Kale Party. A contested 2015 presidential election was annulled, and he won the 2016 rerun before taking office. His presidency unfolded amid political conflict and public distrust of institutions. On July 7, 2021, armed attackers entered his residence and killed him; his wife, Martine Moïse, was wounded. The attack deepened a crisis in a country already struggling with political instability.

key_facts.text: Moïse served as Haiti’s president from February 7, 2017, to July 7, 2021.
He had worked in agriculture before entering presidential politics.
The disputed 2015 presidential vote was annulled; Moïse won the 2016 rerun.
Moïse was assassinated at his residence on July 7, 2021.
His wife, Martine Moïse, was wounded in the attack.

overview.text: The al-Anfal campaign was a series of Iraqi government operations against Kurdish communities in northern Iraq in 1988, during the final year of the Iran–Iraq War. Directed by Ali Hassan al-Majid under Saddam Hussein’s Baathist government, it combined military assaults with village destruction, mass detention, disappearances, forced displacement, and chemical weapons. Iraqi authorities presented the operations as counterinsurgency, but civilians were attacked because they lived in areas designated for removal. Human Rights Watch, drawing on Iraqi records and survivor testimony, concluded that the campaign constituted genocide. The name “Anfal” came from a Quranic chapter, which the government used as its campaign label.

key_facts.text: The campaign ran from late February into September 1988.
Ali Hassan al-Majid directed the operations for Iraq’s Baathist government.
Iraqi forces destroyed villages and forcibly displaced Kurdish residents.
Chemical weapons were used in attacks associated with the campaign.
Human Rights Watch classified the campaign against Kurdish people as genocide.

overview.text: The eighteenth century covers the years 1701 through 1800. Across the Atlantic world, it was an age of expanding imperial commerce, colonial conquest, and slavery, as well as arguments about liberty and political authority. Enlightenment thinkers debated reason, government, and rights; their ideas circulated through books and conversation. Revolutionaries in Britain’s American colonies declared independence in 1776, and the French Revolution began in 1789. The Haitian Revolution began in the French colony of Saint-Domingue in 1791. These struggles revealed a sharp tension between claims of universal freedom and the continued enslavement of millions. George III’s British reign began in 1760 and spanned the American Revolution.

key_facts.text: By conventional numbering, the eighteenth century began in 1701 and ended in 1800.
George III became king of Great Britain in 1760.
The American colonies declared independence in 1776.
The French Revolution began in 1789.
The Haitian Revolution began in Saint-Domingue in 1791.

overview.text: The Nika riots were an uprising in Constantinople, capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, in January 532. Supporters of the Blue and Green chariot-racing factions united against Emperor Justinian I after tensions over punishment, taxation, and imperial rule. Crowds shouted “Nika,” meaning “Conquer,” and unrest spread from the Hippodrome into the city. Buildings burned, including the church that preceded today’s Hagia Sophia. Justinian’s forces eventually crushed the rebellion in the Hippodrome, killing many participants. The destruction also gave Justinian an opportunity to build a new, much larger Hagia Sophia, dedicated in 537. The revolt shows how the arena could become a stage for politics as well as sport.

key_facts.text: The riots took place in Constantinople in January 532 during Justinian I’s reign.
The Blue and Green chariot factions joined in revolt.
“Nika” was a cry meaning “Conquer.”
Imperial forces violently suppressed the uprising at the Hippodrome.
The earlier Hagia Sophia burned; Justinian’s replacement was dedicated in 537.

overview.text: The Boshin War was a Japanese civil war fought in 1868–69 between forces supporting the new imperial government and defenders of the Tokugawa shogunate. A proclamation restoring imperial rule came early in 1868, but it did not settle who would control the country. Imperial forces won the opening battle at Toba-Fushimi near Kyoto. Edo Castle then surrendered through negotiation, sparing the city a major assault, while resistance continued in northeastern Japan. Fighting ended when the last shogunate supporters surrendered at Hakodate on Hokkaido in June 1869. The war consolidated the political change known as the Meiji Restoration rather than beginning that change on its own.

key_facts.text: The Boshin War began with fighting at Toba-Fushimi in January 1868.
The opposing sides supported the imperial government and the Tokugawa shogunate.
Edo Castle surrendered after negotiation instead of a full-scale assault.
Resistance continued in northeastern Japan, including Aizu.
The last shogunate supporters surrendered at Hakodate in June 1869.

overview.text: Gran Colombia was a republic created during the wars for independence from Spain in northern South America. Its official name was the Republic of Colombia; “Gran Colombia” is an unofficial name now used to distinguish it from today’s Colombia. A law adopted at Angostura in 1819 proposed the union, and a constitution followed at Cúcuta in 1821. Simón Bolívar served as its first president. At its greatest extent, the republic included territories corresponding to present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama. Regional political conflicts strained the union, which broke apart by 1831. Its brief history reflects Bolívar’s ambition for a larger independent republic as well as the difficulties of governing such a vast territory.

key_facts.text: The republic’s official name was the Republic of Colombia.
The Angostura law establishing the union was adopted in 1819.
A constitution was adopted at Cúcuta in 1821.
Simón Bolívar became its first president.
Its territory included what are now Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama.

overview.text: Minoan civilization flourished on the island of Crete during the Bronze Age. Its major centers included Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia, where large complexes served administrative, ceremonial, and economic purposes. Surviving frescoes, fine pottery, and evidence of maritime exchange reveal a society connected to the wider Aegean and eastern Mediterranean. Minoans used writing systems known as Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A. The modern name comes from Minos, a king of later Greek legend, and was popularized by archaeologist Arthur Evans. A volcanic eruption devastated Akrotiri on nearby Thera, but it should not be treated as a proven single cause of the changes that later transformed Cretan society.

key_facts.text: Important Cretan palatial centers included Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia.
Minoan administrative writing included Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A.
The name “Minoan” refers to Minos of Greek legend and was popularized by Arthur Evans.
Art and material finds attest to maritime connections beyond Crete.
The Thera eruption buried Akrotiri, a site on Thera rather than Crete.

overview.text: The Satsuma Rebellion was an armed uprising against Japan’s Meiji government in 1877. Its leader, Saigō Takamori, had helped overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and establish the new government, but later became estranged from its leaders. Disaffected former samurai associated with schools in Kagoshima rallied around him. They marched north in February and fought government forces around Kumamoto and elsewhere on Kyushu. The uprising ended after Saigō’s forces were defeated at Shiroyama in September. Resentment over Meiji reforms helped drive the revolt, yet Saigō had once helped build the very government he challenged. The defeat confirmed the new government’s military authority.

key_facts.text: The rebellion began in 1877 under Saigō Takamori.
Saigō had earlier helped bring about the Meiji Restoration.
Rebel forces marched from Kagoshima toward Kumamoto in February.
The final defeat came at Shiroyama in September 1877.
Some former samurai, including men from Aizu, served the government against the rebels.

overview.text: Mexico became independent from Spain in 1821 and established a federal republic under a constitution adopted in 1824. During the nineteenth century, it faced internal political conflict, war with the United States, and French intervention. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the U.S.–Mexican War and transferred extensive territory to the United States. French-backed Maximilian ruled a short-lived Mexican empire before republican forces defeated him in 1867. In the early twentieth century, revolution produced a new constitution in 1917. That same year, Germany’s Zimmermann Telegram proposed an alliance with Mexico against the United States, promising support for recovering lost territory. The message became part of the diplomatic crisis surrounding U.S. entry into World War I.

key_facts.text: Mexico became independent from Spain in 1821.
The 1824 constitution established a federal republic.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the U.S.–Mexican War in 1848.
Maximilian’s French-backed empire fell in 1867.
Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico in the 1917 Zimmermann Telegram.
